plan.chapterName: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 5.3.4
plan.contextChunk: This figure contains two panels, (a) and (b), illustrating the shell method for computing volumes of solids of revolution about the y-axis. Panel (a): the 2D xy-plane showing a decreasing curve with a single rectangular strip Rk spanning from x_{k-1} to xk approximating the kth vertical strip of the region; a rotation arrow near the y-axis indicates revolution about that axis. Caption: Rectangle approximating the kth strip. Panel (b): a 3D view of the cylindrical shell Sk generated by revolving the rectangle about the y-axis, shown as a hollow cylindrical ring. Caption: Cylindrical shell generated by the rectangle. The figure introduces the shell method by showing how each thin vertical rectangle, when revolved, produces a cylindrical shell whose volume approximates the corresponding tubular portion of the solid.

elements: y-axis (vertical axis of revolution) with arrowhead and label y
x-axis (horizontal) with arrowhead and label x
decreasing smooth curve y = f(x) (teal) above the x-axis
region under the curve between x = a and x = b (light shaded)
n thin vertical rectangles approximating the region (panel a)
highlighted kth rectangle Rk spanning x_{k-1} to x_k (darker teal fill)
curved rotation arrow near the y-axis indicating revolution
cylindrical shell Sk: hollow ring obtained by revolving Rk about the y-axis (panel b)
full set of n concentric thin shells forming the solid of revolution (semi-transparent grey)
labels x_{k-1}, x_k on the x-axis; Rk inside the rectangle; Sk beside the shell
readout of shell radius, height, and volume for Sk

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: Switching between the flat rectangle and its revolved shell makes the 2D-to-3D correspondence concrete: one vertical strip sweeps out one cylindrical shell about the y-axis

interactions.label: Strip index k
interactions.teaches: Selecting different strips shows that shells nearer the axis are short and thin while outer shells are taller or shorter per f(x), so each shell contributes radius-dependent volume 2π·r·h·Δx

interactions.label: Number of strips n
interactions.teaches: Increasing n thins every shell and the sum of shell volumes converges to the true volume of the solid — the Riemann sum becoming the integral ∫2πx f(x)dx
Rotating the 3D view reveals that the shell is a hollow tube of thickness Δx whose inner and outer radii are x_{k-1} and x_k, not a flat slab

demo_steps.title: One strip, one shell
demo_steps.narration: With n = 6, the kth rectangle Rk is highlighted between x_{k-1} and x_k. Toggle to the revolved view to see it sweep out the hollow cylindrical shell Sk.

demo_steps.title: Inspect the shell in 3D
demo_steps.narration: In the revolved view, drag to orbit: Sk is a thin-walled tube of radius ≈ x_k and height ≈ f(x_k); its volume is approximately 2π·radius·height·thickness.

demo_steps.title: Refine the approximation
demo_steps.narration: Raise n toward 20: the shells become thinner, the jagged union smooths into the true solid of revolution, and the displayed shell-volume sum approaches the exact volume.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use f(x) = 2 + 1.5·exp(-0.35(x-1)) − small linear falloff, or simply f(x) = 3.2 − 0.18x² on x ∈ [1, 4] (monotone decreasing, f(1)=3.02, f(4)=0.32), matching the source's gently falling teal curve. World units: x-axis runs 0 to 5 along +X, y-axis 0 to 4 along +Y, origin at axes intersection. Flat view (a): axes drawn straight-on, curve as teal #17a2a8 line, n rectangles spanning [a,b]=[1,4] with equal Δx=(b−a)/n, each of height f at its right endpoint; the kth rectangle filled teal #9fd8d4 at 0.6 opacity with dark outline, labelled Rk; small curved arrow around the y-axis above origin. Revolved view (b): same axes in 3D; solid of revolution rendered as a semi-transparent grey #c8c8c8 (opacity ~0.35) surface of revolution of f about the y-axis; all n shells shown as nested rings with thin edges, and shell Sk highlighted in teal #17a2a8 (opacity ~0.7) with inner radius x_{k−1}, outer radius x_k, height f(x_k), sitting on the x-axis plane. The teal curve trace appears on the shell/solid surface as in the source. Readout panel: radius r = (x_{k−1}+x_k)/2, height h = f(x_k), ΔV = 2πrhΔx, plus running total ΣΔV vs exact V = ∫₁⁴ 2πx f(x)dx (exact ≈ 2π·[1.6x² − 0.045x⁴]₁⁴ = 2π(1.6·15 − 0.045·255) ≈ 2π·12.52 ≈ 78.7). Position of Sk label: right side of the highlighted shell, matching source.
interactionPlan.notes: Build shells as THREE.CylinderGeometry with open-ended theta slices or LatheGeometry rings; use side: THREE.DoubleSide and depthWrite false for the translucent solid so nested shells stay visible. On stripIndex change, animate the highlight moving between shells (fade old, raise opacity on new) rather than rebuilding geometry. In flat view, render the scene with an orthographic-feel frontal camera (or keep perspective with low FOV); in revolved view enable orbit controls with damping. Keep both views sharing one scene graph: the flat rectangles are the same meshes that extrude/revolve into shells on toggle, reinforcing the correspondence.

authoredContext: As a rule, the tubes will have curved upper surfaces, so there will be no simple formulas for their volumes. However, if the strips are thin, then we can approximate each strip by a rectangle (Figure 5.3.4a). These rectangles, when revolved about the y-axis, will produce cylindrical shells whose volumes closely approximate the volumes of the tubes generated by the original strips (Figure 5.3.4b). We will show that by adding the volumes of the cylindrical shells we can obtain a Riemann sum that approximates the volume V, and by taking the limit of the Riemann sums we can obtain an integral for the exact volume V .

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use f(x) = 2 + 1.5·exp(-0.35(x-1)) − small linear falloff, or simply f(x) = 3.2 − 0.18x² on x ∈ [1, 4] (monotone decreasing, f(1)=3.02, f(4)=0.32), matching the source's gently falling teal curve. World units: x-axis runs 0 to 5 along +X, y-axis 0 to 4 along +Y, origin at axes intersection. Flat view (a): axes drawn straight-on, curve as teal #17a2a8 line, n rectangles spanning [a,b]=[1,4] with equal Δx=(b−a)/n, each of height f at its right endpoint; the kth rectangle filled teal #9fd8d4 at 0.6 opacity with dark outline, labelled Rk; small curved arrow around the y-axis above origin. Revolved view (b): same axes in 3D; solid of revolution rendered as a semi-transparent grey #c8c8c8 (opacity ~0.35) surface of revolution of f about the y-axis; all n shells shown as nested rings with thin edges, and shell Sk highlighted in teal #17a2a8 (opacity ~0.7) with inner radius x_{k−1}, outer radius x_k, height f(x_k), sitting on the x-axis plane. The teal curve trace appears on the shell/solid surface as in the source. Readout panel: radius r = (x_{k−1}+x_k)/2, height h = f(x_k), ΔV = 2πrhΔx, plus running total ΣΔV vs exact V = ∫₁⁴ 2πx f(x)dx (exact ≈ 2π·[1.6x² − 0.045x⁴]₁⁴ = 2π(1.6·15 − 0.045·255) ≈ 2π·12.52 ≈ 78.7). Position of Sk label: right side of the highlighted shell, matching source.
interactionPlan.notes: Build shells as THREE.CylinderGeometry with open-ended theta slices or LatheGeometry rings; use side: THREE.DoubleSide and depthWrite false for the translucent solid so nested shells stay visible. On stripIndex change, animate the highlight moving between shells (fade old, raise opacity on new) rather than rebuilding geometry. In flat view, render the scene with an orthographic-feel frontal camera (or keep perspective with low FOV); in revolved view enable orbit controls with damping. Keep both views sharing one scene graph: the flat rectangles are the same meshes that extrude/revolve into shells on toggle, reinforcing the correspondence.

plan.authoredPrompt: This figure contains two panels, (a) and (b), illustrating the shell method for computing volumes of solids of revolution about the y-axis. Panel (a): the 2D xy-plane showing a decreasing curve with a single rectangular strip Rk spanning from x_{k-1} to xk approximating the kth vertical strip of the region; a rotation arrow near the y-axis indicates revolution about that axis. Caption: Rectangle approximating the kth strip. Panel (b): a 3D view of the cylindrical shell Sk generated by revolving the rectangle about the y-axis, shown as a hollow cylindrical ring. Caption: Cylindrical shell generated by the rectangle. The figure introduces the shell method by showing how each thin vertical rectangle, when revolved, produces a cylindrical shell whose volume approximates the corresponding tubular portion of the solid.
plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for strip index k: select the kth rectangle in panel (a) and simultaneously highlight the corresponding cylindrical shell Sₖ in panel (b), displaying its radius, height, and volume
- Slider for number of strips n: increase n and watch the shells become thinner, with the total shell volume sum converging to the true solid volume
- Drag to rotate the 3D cylindrical shell in panel (b) to inspect its geometry from any angle
plan.sourcePath: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 5.3.4
